title: Improving dual targeting selectivity in T-cell engagers via synapse-gated and affinity-tuned trispecific antibody design
one_line: The authors engineer trispecific T-cell engagers that require co-engagement of two tumour antigens plus CD3, using affinity tuning and synapse-gated design to improve selectivity for dual-antigen-positive cells over single-antigen-positive normal tissue.
key_claims: Dual tumour-antigen targeting combined with CD3 engagement in a single trispecific format can increase killing selectivity for double-positive cells relative to conventional bispecific T-cell engagers.
Selectivity is claimed to depend on affinity tuning of the individual binding arms, with lower-affinity arms relying on avidity from co-engagement to reach a killing threshold.
A 'synapse-gated' geometry/format is claimed to contribute to selectivity independently of raw affinity, implying format design is a separate lever from binding strength.
No specific quantitative values (affinities, EC50s, selectivity windows) were captured in the episode notes, so numbers should be pulled from the paper before citing.
limitations: The episode notes contain only the DOI, so no in-paper numbers, cell lines, or model systems were recorded here.
Selectivity gains of this type are typically shown in vitro on engineered antigen-density panels; in vivo and normal-tissue safety evidence is not documented in the notes.
Affinity-tuned engagers can trade selectivity for potency, and the magnitude of that trade-off is not captured here.
Manufacturability, stability, and pharmacokinetics of the trispecific format are not recorded.
open_questions: Does the synapse-gated trispecific spare single-antigen-positive primary human normal cells at doses that clear double-positive tumour in vivo?
How narrow is the antigen-density window over which selectivity holds, and does antigen loss or downregulation collapse it?
Can the selectivity benefit be separated cleanly from simple affinity attenuation by testing matched-affinity non-gated controls?
